case_study_insert.main_stem: Ellersby Industrial Pumps (EIP) is a workers' cooperative in the industrial pump manufacturing sector in West Yorkshire, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2007 by Fatima Ellersby, it makes centrifugal pumps for water treatment and process plants and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. EIP plans to invest $540,000 in a new pump-testing facility, financed by a $300,000 retained surplus and a $240,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.00 a unit and a selling price of $13.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. EIP faces a quality problem: customer complaints about pump seals have risen and the defect rate is 3.5%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Market Research Summary — Q4 2025: The plant tested 12,600 pumps last quarter at a seal-defect rate of 3.5%, up from 2.1% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 17 to 34 per month. Average fulfilment time lengthened to 8 days from 5 days. Research among 300 water-treatment buyers found that 55% would pay up to $0.60 more for a certified leak-free pump, and 44% check service records before ordering. A skills audit shows 14 of 64 members lack pump-test certification; on-the-job mentoring is available, while off-the-job college courses cost $680 per member.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $13.40 to $14.27 per hour from April 2026, raising engineering wage bills. (3) Cast iron and motor input costs have risen 8.9% year-on-year, while water-treatment plant spending grew 4.2%.

questions.question_text: EIP plans to fund part of its $540,000 testing facility with a $240,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for EIP of using the $300,000 retained surplus instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The retained surplus carries no interest or capital repayments, so EIP avoids new debt service on top of fixed costs of $180,000 a year. That protects the cooperative's cash flow while the $540,000 pump-testing facility is built and helps absorb the 6.5% minimum wage rise and the 8.9% rise in cast iron and motor costs without raising the $13.00 price. Cash not paid to a lender stays available for the 14 members needing certification training.

Point 2: Using the retained surplus keeps decision-making inside the cooperative, so the 64 member-workers control how the testing facility is run without a lender imposing repayment conditions or taking security over the plant. Unlike the $240,000 bank loan, there is no repossession risk if water-treatment orders slip, and the surplus can be combined flexibly with the borrowing rather than locked into a fixed schedule. This matters when the 3.5% defect rate is already pushing complaints up from 17 to 34 a month.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to EIP and its $540,000 financing decision.

questions.question_text: EIP is promoting its certified leak-free pumps. Consider advertising in water-industry journals, exhibiting at an environmental technology show, or using social media to reach water-treatment engineers. Which should EIP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Advertising in water-industry journals: Print adverts would reach procurement staff at water-treatment firms and give credibility to the certified leak-free claim. The drawback is cost and poor targeting: many readers will not buy centrifugal pumps, and a cooperative with fixed costs of $180,000 a year and a $540,000 testing facility cannot afford much wasted spend, nor can it easily measure enquiries.

Environmental technology exhibition: A stand lets engineers inspect the pumps and question EIP about the 3.5% seal-defect rate and the new testing facility. It suits the 44% of surveyed buyers who check service records, because staff can show test certificates on the spot. The limits are stand cost, a short event window and the need for rapid follow-up with the 300 buyers in the research sample.

Social media for water-treatment engineers: Targeted posts can reach the 55% of buyers who would pay $0.60 more for a certified leak-free pump, at low cost and with measurable clicks. It is fast and suits a small 64-member team, but technical buyers often want physical proof of seal quality before switching, so social media alone may generate interest rather than firm orders.

Recommendation: EIP should choose the environmental technology exhibition as the primary channel, supported by low-cost social media. Face-to-face inspection best answers concern about the 3.5% defect rate and reaches the engineers in the 44% who check records. Journal advertising is rejected as untargeted and unmeasurable for a small cooperative; social media alone is rejected because engineers need to see the certified pump, so it should support rather than replace the exhibition.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with minimal application to EIP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of EIP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of EIP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why journal advertising and social media alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: EIP's pump-seal defect rate is 3.5% and complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for EIP of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its 64 members.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership fits a cooperative and gives the 64 member-workers a say in how the new pump-testing facility operates, satisfying social and esteem needs and raising job satisfaction. Members who help set testing routines are more likely to take care over seal fitting, directly attacking the 3.5% defect rate and the complaints that have risen from 17 to 34 a month. In Maslow's terms, participation meets higher-order needs that a wage rise alone cannot.

Point 2: Consulting the members who build and test pumps generates practical fixes that managers alone would miss, improving quality without extra capital beyond the $540,000 facility. Herzberg would view the added responsibility as a motivator, so members take pride in the certified leak-free pump. Higher involvement strengthens commitment in the flat structure, reducing the need to replace staff and the $680 per member training cost, and protecting output of 90,000 pumps while the testing facility is commissioned and the 8-day fulfilment time is reduced.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to EIP's defect rate, complaints, workforce and training costs.

questions.question_text: EIP must train 14 members to certify pumps in the new facility. Consider on-the-job mentoring or off-the-job college courses at $680 per member. Which should EIP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job mentoring: Mentoring at the West Yorkshire plant is specific to EIP's own pumps and test procedures, avoids the $680 per member fee for 14 staff, a saving of $9,520 (14 × $680), and keeps members productive while they learn. That protects the 12,600 pumps tested last quarter and helps cut the 3.5% defect rate. The drawbacks are that mentors are taken off their own work, bad habits can spread, and there is no external certificate, which matters when 44% of buyers check service records before ordering.

Off-the-job college courses: At $680 each, 14 members cost $9,520, affordable against the $540,000 investment and easy to timetable away from the shop floor. College provides structured teaching and a recognised certificate, valuable given the rise in complaints from 17 to 34 a month and the 55% who would pay $0.60 more for certified pumps. However, members leave the shop floor, reducing capacity in the new testing facility, and generic content may not match EIP's exact test methods, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: EIP should choose on-the-job mentoring first, with short external modules for the lead testers. Mentoring is cheaper, pump-specific and avoids losing output while defects are 3.5%. Full off-the-job training is rejected because removing 14 of 64 members and spending $9,520 would slow commissioning of the $540,000 facility and still need on-site reinforcement; certification can be added once the facility is running smoothly and the 8-day fulfilment time is brought down. The $9,520 saved also helps cover $180,000 of fixed costs while the 8-day fulfilment time is improved.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to EIP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of EIP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of EIP with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how EIP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($13.00 − $7.00) = $180,000 ÷ $6.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $13.00 − $7.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways EIP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 90,000 pumps gives a margin of safety of 60,000 units, showing the cooperative can cover the $540,000 testing facility well before capacity is reached.
2. Contribution of $6.00 a pump lets EIP test the $0.60 premium for certified leak-free pumps; if accepted by the 55% of buyers, contribution would rise to $6.60 and the $180,000 fixed costs would be recovered sooner.
3. Fixed costs of $180,000 and $6.00 contribution show the extra volume needed to service the $240,000 bank loan, so member-managers can set a sales target for water-treatment plants.
4. Average total cost of $9.00 a pump ($180,000 ÷ 90,000 = $2.00 plus $7.00) can be benchmarked each quarter to detect the waste behind the 3.5% seal-defect rate and to monitor the $7.00 variable cost as cast iron and motor prices rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 90,000-unit output; certified-pump premium modelling; loan-service volume for the $240,000 borrowing; and average total cost of $9.00 to monitor defects.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate EIP's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has EIP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.67 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.04 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.14 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $60,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $40,000 cash = $195,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $88,000 + $62,000 = $220,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 = $195,000 ÷ $130,000 = 1.50 and 2025 = $220,000 ÷ $132,000 = 1.67. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($195,000 − $60,000) ÷ $130,000 = $135,000 ÷ $130,000 = 1.04; 2025 = ($220,000 − $70,000) ÷ $132,000 = $150,000 ÷ $132,000 = 1.14.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The current ratio rose from 1.50 to 1.67 as current assets grew from $195,000 to $220,000 while current liabilities were nearly flat at $130,000 and $132,000. The acid test also improved from 1.04 to 1.14, so the cooperative is less dependent on selling inventory to pay short-term debts, which is helpful while it repays a $240,000 bank loan and spends $540,000 on the testing facility. Cash rose from $40,000 to $62,000 and receivables fell from $95,000 to $88,000, a healthy sign. The one caution is inventories rising from $60,000 to $70,000; with a 3.5% seal-defect rate, some of that stock may be slow-moving.

Conclusion: EIP's financial position has improved. Both the current ratio (1.50 to 1.67) and the acid test (1.04 to 1.14) show stronger short-term solvency, and cash growth supports the improvement rather than inventory buildup. The main watch item is the $70,000 of inventories, so the cooperative should monitor stock quality while investing in the testing facility.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether liquidity improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for EIP of introducing a quality-assurance programme to reduce its 3.5% seal-defect rate.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A prevention-focused quality-assurance programme should lower the 3.5% seal-defect rate and the complaints that rose from 17 to 34 a month. That protects the $6.00 contribution on each $13.00 pump and lets EIP pursue the 55% of buyers who would pay $0.60 more for a certified leak-free pump, strengthening returns from the $540,000 testing facility. It also supports the 44% who check service records, because documented checks reassure them before ordering.

Disadvantage: Establishing quality assurance needs training for the 14 members and may slow output of 90,000 pumps while procedures are introduced, raising unit costs on top of $180,000 fixed costs. Because the insert does not quantify the cost of rework or inspection, the net benefit cannot be proven, and the flat structure may find it hard to enforce consistent standards across all 64 members. With fulfilment already at 8 days, any extra checking could lengthen delivery and weaken the 44% service-focused group.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to EIP's defect rate, research data and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 8.9% rise in cast iron and motor input costs will affect EIP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If EIP's $240,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by the 0.75 percentage-point rise × $240,000 = $1,800 a year (0.0075 × $240,000). This is small beside fixed costs of $180,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Higher rates could also make water-treatment customers delay capital projects, but EIP can largely remove the direct risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $14.27 an hour): The insert gives a workforce of 64 but not hours worked, individual pay or how many members are on the minimum, so a defensible annual wage bill cannot be invented. The derived figure is labour productivity: 90,000 pumps ÷ 64 staff = 1,406.25 pumps per worker. If that holds, the rise is manageable; if the 3.5% defect rate or absence reduces output, unit labour cost climbs and the $6.00 contribution per pump narrows. The effect is real but cannot be precisely quantified from the data.

Input cost inflation (8.9% on cast iron and motors): The insert does not decompose the $7.00 variable cost, so only an explicitly labelled upper bound is honest: if the entire $7.00 rose 8.9%, that adds 8.9% × $7.00 = $0.62 per pump, and across 90,000 pumps a year that is $55,800 (90,000 × $0.62). Even a partial increase compounds over all output and cuts contribution below $6.00, though the $0.60 certified-pump premium found in the research could offset part of it.

Conclusion: The 8.9% rise in cast iron and motor inputs will have the greatest impact. Its $55,800 bound exceeds the $1,800 interest effect, it touches every one of the 90,000 pumps, and it directly erodes the $6.00 contribution needed to cover $180,000 fixed costs. The interest rise is small and hedgeable by fixing the rate; the wage rise cannot be quantified from the insert and can be partly absorbed through productivity of 1,406.25 pumps per worker.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to EIP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on EIP with shown calculations where data allow.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of EIP using only shown derivations from insert figures and a well-justified greatest-impact judgment.
